content.text: Book reference: Chapter 17, pages 599–657. The book's own five review labs (Managing Files, Users/Groups/Permissions/Processes, Configuring and Managing a Server, Managing Networks, Mounting File Systems and Finding Files) exist to re-exercise every chapter's skills together rather than in isolation. This section rebuilds that same integrated practice using your own lab, plus a full exam-objectives map and an exam-day checklist to close out this guide.
Cross-referencing every chapter of this guide against what it actually covers — use this table to triage remaining study time toward whatever still feels shaky.
| Domain | Chapters | Priority |
| Lab environment & registration | Part 0, Ch 14 | Foundational |
| Command line, files, text editing | Ch 2, 3, 4, 5 | Exam-critical |
| Users, groups, permissions | Ch 6, 7 | Exam-critical |
| Processes & services | Ch 8, 9 | Exam-critical |
| SSH & logging | Ch 10, 11 | Exam-critical |
| Networking & file transfer | Ch 12, 13 | Exam-critical |
| Software & storage | Ch 14, 15 | Exam-critical |
| Web Console, Portal, Insights | Ch 16 | Awareness only — not graded hands-on |
If time is short before exam day, this is the condensed set worth being fluent in without hesitation — pulled from every "EXAM CRITICAL" callout across this guide.
| Domain | Commands |
| Files | `mkdir -p, cp -r, mv, rm -r, ln / ln -s, find (with -name/-perm/-size/-mmin/-type)` |
| Users & groups | `useradd, usermod -aG, userdel -r, groupadd, chage, passwd` |
| Permissions | `chmod (symbolic and octal), chown user:group, special perms (u+s/g+s/o+t, leading 4/2/1)` |
| Processes | `ps aux, jobs/bg/fg, kill -15 then -9, pgrep/pkill` |
| Services | `systemctl status/start/stop/restart/reload/enable/disable/mask --now` |
| SSH | `ssh-keygen, ssh-copy-id, PermitRootLogin, PasswordAuthentication` |
| Logs | `journalctl -p/-b/-u/--since, Storage=persistent` |
| Networking | `nmcli con mod/up/down, nmcli dev disconnect, hostnamectl set-hostname` |
| Transfer | `tar -czf/-xzf, scp, rsync -av (mind the trailing slash)` |
| Software | `dnf search/install/remove/history, rpm -qf, dnf config-manager` |
| Storage | `lsblk -fp, mount UUID=, df -h, du -h` |

A single connected exercise touching most chapters at once, run entirely on your own servera/serverb — deliberately similar in spirit to the book's five review labs, without needing any grading script.

1. Users & groups (Ch 6, 7) — On servera: create users opuser1 and opuser2, a group named opteam (fixed GID), add both users to it with usermod -aG. Create a shared directory /shared/opteam owned by root:opteam with setgid and 2770 permissions. Confirm a file created by opuser1 inside it is automatically group-owned by opteam.
2. Processes (Ch 8) — As opuser1, start a background sleep 600 &, note its PID, then from another session use pgrep -l -u opuser1 to find it and pkill -u opuser1 to clean it up.

3. Services (Ch 9) — Pick any installed-but-inactive service; enable --now it, confirm with systemctl is-active and is-enabled, then reload (or restart) it and confirm the PID behavior matches what you'd expect.
4. SSH (Ch 10) — Generate a fresh keypair for opuser1, ssh-copy-id it to serverb, confirm passwordless login works, then set PermitRootLogin no on serverb and confirm root SSH login is refused.
5. Logs (Ch 11) — journalctl -u sshd --since "-10 min" on serverb to see the login attempts you just generated; confirm Storage=persistent is set and survives a reboot.
6. Networking (Ch 12) — Confirm serverb's static IP and hostname still match Part 0's plan with ip addr and hostnamectl; getent hosts each of the other three lab machines to confirm name resolution.
7. Transfer (Ch 13) — tar -czf a backup of /shared/opteam on servera, scp it to serverb, then extract it there and diff -r the two directory trees to confirm they match exactly.
8. Software (Ch 14) — dnf install a small real package on serverb, rpm -ql it to see what it placed on disk, then dnf remove it and confirm with rpm -q that it's gone.
9. Storage & find (Ch 15) — lsblk -fp on servera to find your root file system's UUID; find /shared -type f -perm -002 to confirm nothing in your shared directory is accidentally world-writable.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Why one integrated exercise beats re-reading nine separate chapters

The real exam presents scenarios, not chapter labels — a single task might quietly require you to create a user, set permissions, and verify with a service restart, all without saying which chapter each part came from. Practicing chapters in combination, the way this scenario does, is a closer rehearsal of exam conditions than reviewing each skill in isolation one more time.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Read every task twice before typing anything

The single most common reason for losing exam points isn't lack of skill — it's misreading what was actually asked (wrong hostname, wrong username, wrong permission value) under time pressure. Read the full task, then read it again, before your first keystroke.

1. Confirm which machine you're on before running anything — hostname or a glance at the prompt, every single time you switch terminals. A perfectly correct command run on the wrong server is a wrong answer.
2. Save changes as you go: after any config edit, verify it immediately (systemctl status, systemctl reload, a fresh SSH connection) rather than batching verification to the end.
3. For every enable/disable + start/stop pair, do both halves explicitly, or use --now / disable --now — don't assume one implies the other (Chapter 9's most common mistake).
4. Before any rm -r, tar extraction, or rsync, double check pwd and the exact paths involved — there's no undo on any of these.
5. man <command> is available and allowed — use it rather than guessing an option under pressure; you already practiced fast navigation in Chapter 4.
6. If a task depends on a previous task's result (a common exam pattern — e.g. a user created earlier needs a permission set later), verify the earlier step actually succeeded before building on it.

7. Reboot-test anything that's supposed to survive a reboot (persistent journal, enabled services, static network config) if time allows — a change that LOOKS applied but wasn't saved to the right file won't survive, and you want to find that out before the exam ends, not after.
8. Leave a few minutes at the end to re-read the task list once more against what you actually did, rather than stopping the moment you think you're finished.

This guide followed the book chapter by chapter, verified every command against either the book's own text or Red Hat's official behavior, and flagged the one substitution needed (Chapter 14's classroom content server) explicitly rather than leaving it as a silent gap. The lab environment built in Part 0 stays useful well past this course too — the same four machines are the foundation for RH134 and beyond, so there's no need to tear anything down.
All 17 chapters plus the environment build are complete in this document — nothing from the book's own table of contents was skipped.
Every EXAM CRITICAL callout across the guide is what Section 17.2's command table condenses down to, if a single pre-exam skim is all the remaining time allows.
Good luck on the RHCSA — the lab you built is the same one the material was written for, and every command in here has been run, not just described.
